strengths: The central idea—replacing position-specific multi-token targets with a compact summary of a longer future—is intuitive, relevant, and potentially useful for improving pretraining objectives.

The paper studies both a simple bag-of-tokens target and a learned reverse-LM representation, and the synthetic path-star and sibling-discovery experiments provide helpful intuition about horizon length and irrelevant future information.

Experiments are conducted at substantial 3B- and 8B-parameter scales, with identical training data across the compared student models and evaluations spanning reasoning, mathematics, and code generation.
FSP-RevLM produces encouraging 8B results, including improvements over standard MTP on all six reported benchmarks and particularly strong ARC-Easy, MATH, and MBPP results.
weaknesses: The main comparison is not compute-controlled. FSP-RevLM requires training a separate reverse LM on the full corpus, apparently adding roughly another complete pretraining run, yet this cost is excluded. The claim that it is amortized is insufficient without demonstrating reuse across students or reporting total training, teacher-inference, storage, and wall-clock costs. Consequently, the gains cannot be attributed cleanly to the objective rather than substantially greater compute and supervision.

The large-scale MTP comparison is weak: MTP and DS-MTP are restricted to only one auxiliary future head because FSP uses one head. This is not an equal-compute comparison and omits stronger multi-head configurations and relevant recent future-prediction/bidirectional baselines. The very poor 8B DS-MTP ARC results also warrant investigation.

The evaluation protocol selects the best temperature separately for every method and task and then reports test performance, with no validation-based selection procedure described. This introduces test-set tuning and multiple-comparison bias. Reporting pass@16 rather than standard pass@1 or greedy accuracy further makes it unclear whether FSP improves the model's core capability or mainly sampling diversity.

Essential implementation details are missing, including the auxiliary-loss coefficient, optimizer and warmup settings, architecture and tokenizer specifications, reverse-model checkpoint selection, target normalization or projection, and whether teacher representations are computed online or cached. Dataset mixture weights, prompts, answer extraction, and benchmark contamination controls are also absent, substantially limiting reproducibility.

The meaning of the reported three seeds is unclear. Near-zero or exactly zero standard errors on ARC are difficult to reconcile with three independent 8B pretraining runs; if these are only decoding seeds, the tables do not measure training variance. Several claimed improvements also overlap in uncertainty or are small relative to the strongest baseline.

The evidence does not adequately support the broader long-horizon and reduced-teacher-forcing claims. There is no long-form planning, narrative, or creative-generation evaluation, no direct measure of exposure bias, and no analysis showing that reverse-LM states selectively retain predictable information. On the synthetic sibling task, convergence is not operationally defined and the reverse model has privileged access to the relevant parent token by construction.

The empirical conclusions are overstated: at 3B, FSP-RevLM loses to DS-MTP on four of six tasks; at 8B it loses to NTP on GSM8K and merely ties MTP on HumanEval+. The paper also lacks language-modeling loss/perplexity, training stability, throughput, memory, and total-compute comparisons. Overall, the promising idea and expensive experiments are outweighed by fairness, evaluation-validity, and reproducibility problems.

strengths: The manuscript presents a clear and intuitive idea: supervise a causal language model using a compact representation of its longer-term future rather than separate position-specific future-token predictions. The distinction between bag-of-words and learned reverse-LM summaries is easy to understand. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/7e9156ddf4d14efba0e050892a5bb7fe/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The path-star and modified sibling-discovery experiments provide useful controlled illustrations of when long-range summaries may help and when indiscriminate aggregation becomes noisy.

Experiments at 3B and 8B parameters and up to 1T training tokens represent a substantial empirical investment. The paper compares NTP, standard MTP, DeepSeek-MTP, random future targets, bag-of-words targets, and learned targets.
At 8B scale, FSP-RevLM produces encouraging results on ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, MBPP, and MATH relative to the reported baselines. The manuscript is generally well organized and readable.
weaknesses: The central comparison is not compute-fair. FSP-RevLM requires training a second reverse 8B model on the same 1T-token corpus and apparently running it to generate hidden-state targets. The paper simply excludes the teacher's training cost, arguing that it can be amortized, without demonstrating reuse across students or reporting target-generation, storage, wall-clock, FLOP, or memory costs. This substantially undermines claims of scalability and efficiency.

The MTP baselines are artificially constrained to one auxiliary head to match FSP's head count. That is not necessarily a fair comparison of methods or compute, particularly when the paper's central claim concerns long-horizon supervision. The real-world experiments lack compute- or parameter-matched multi-head MTP and direct comparisons to the cited register, leap-MTP, or TRELAWNEY-style long-range alternatives. The small synthetic appendix with at most four MTP heads does not resolve this issue.

The evaluation protocol is weak for the strength of the claims. Only six downstream benchmarks are reported, with no held-out language-modeling loss, perplexity, broad knowledge evaluation, long-form generation, or direct planning/coherence evaluation. For code and mathematics, the authors select the best temperature separately for every method and test task from 11 candidates; absent a validation set, this is test-set tuning. Reporting primarily pass@16 further obscures greedy or pass@1 quality.

The empirical advantage is inconsistent. At 3B, FSP-RevLM loses to DeepSeek-MTP on four of six tasks and is essentially tied with NTP on MATH. At 8B it remains worse than NTP on GSM8K, ties MTP on HumanEval+, and several improvements are small relative to the reported uncertainty. No significance tests or aggregate analysis are provided. The claim that FSP-RevLM outperforms MTP across all tasks is therefore inaccurate.

The reported uncertainty is insufficiently explained. The paper says results are means over three seeds but does not clarify whether these are three full pretraining runs or merely evaluation-sampling seeds; the many standard errors shown as exactly 0.000 make this especially important. If only decoding seeds vary, the tables do not measure training variability.

The claimed mechanism is not convincingly established. FSP still trains exclusively on ground-truth prefixes, so describing it as substantially reducing teacher forcing conflates additional future supervision with exposure to self-generated histories. There is no direct exposure-bias evaluation, representation analysis, or ablation establishing that the reverse-LM state filters unpredictable information rather than merely providing generic bidirectional distillation.

Important implementation details are missing: the auxiliary-loss coefficient and normalization, precise auxiliary-head architecture, selected reverse-LM layer and state normalization, whether the teacher is frozen, how teacher states are generated or cached, optimizer and scheduler details, tokenizer, exact data-mixture proportions and filtering, prompting templates, decoding limits, and evaluation harness. These omissions prevent meaningful reproduction of the headline experiments.

The synthetic evidence is narrow and partly tailored to the proposed summaries. FSP-BCE receives the unordered set of every target-path node on path-star, making perfect performance unsurprising, while no harder graph families, distribution shifts, compute-matched alternatives, or sensitivity analyses are presented. The sibling experiment reports an underspecified convergence threshold rather than final sample-efficiency curves.

The related-work positioning is too narrow for a representation-prediction/distillation objective, and the paper does not discuss dataset contamination, licensing, privacy, bias, or the environmental cost of training an additional multi-billion-parameter reverse model. Overall, the idea and large-scale evidence are promising, but the fairness, evaluation, reproducibility, and mechanistic gaps are too substantial for acceptance at a top-tier venue.

strengths: Future Summary Prediction is an intuitive and potentially valuable alternative to predicting individual future tokens: it supplies long-horizon supervision through one auxiliary head, and the learned reverse-LM summaries are more expressive than a fixed bag-of-tokens target.

The synthetic path-star and sibling-discovery experiments provide useful controlled evidence for two design motivations: summaries should cover distant future information while suppressing irrelevant future content.

The empirical scale is a notable strength. The paper reports 3B models trained on 250B tokens and 8B models trained on 1T tokens, compares against NTP, MTP, and DeepSeek-MTP, and generally reports means and standard errors over three seeds.

At 8B scale, FSP-RevLM produces credible improvements over standard MTP on all six reported benchmarks and over NTP on five of six, with particularly clear gains on ARC and MATH. The paper also reports less favorable 3B results rather than concealing them.

Ablations covering handcrafted summaries, future-window length, random future-token targets, reverse-model layer depth, and TF-IDF weighting help establish that the form of future supervision matters.
The manuscript is clearly organized, visually polished, and places the approach in relation to MTP, bidirectional modeling, and other future-token objectives.
weaknesses: The central comparison is not compute-matched. FSP-RevLM requires training an additional reverse LM on the full corpus, approximately doubling the major pretraining work relative to NTP/MTP before student training costs are considered. Calling this cost amortized does not demonstrate that it is negligible or reusable, and no equal-compute or equal-total-token comparison is provided.

Important implementation details are missing: the auxiliary-loss coefficient, precise forward and reverse architectures, auxiliary-head size and parameter counts, how a single vector is selected from the reverse LM's sequence of hidden states, target normalization, optimization details for the reverse teacher, and corpus mixture proportions. Equation 7 also omits an explicit aggregation over positions. These omissions substantially limit reproducibility.

The real-world MTP and DeepSeek-MTP baselines are restricted to one auxiliary head. Although this matches the number of heads, it does not match total training compute or exploit the configurations for which MTP was designed. Multi-head MTP is tested only on the small synthetic problem, leaving the main large-scale comparison incomplete.

The evaluation is narrower than the paper's broad claims about long-horizon reasoning, planning, narrative coherence, and creative writing. It includes only six conventional benchmarks, with no direct long-form generation, planning, coherence, perplexity, or held-out pretraining-loss evaluation.

For code and mathematics, the authors select the best temperature separately for every method and task using the evaluated benchmark. Without a distinct validation protocol, this constitutes test-set hyperparameter selection and can inflate pass@16 comparisons. Data-contamination controls are also not discussed despite training on broad web, code, and reasoning corpora.

Results are mixed rather than uniformly compelling: at 3B, DeepSeek-MTP wins four of six tasks; at 8B, NTP remains best on GSM8K, while the HumanEval+ result only ties MTP. Several differences have overlapping standard errors, but no paired significance analysis is given.

The claimed mechanism remains under-validated. The paper asserts that learned summaries retain predictable, relevant future information, but provides no representation analysis, probing, alternative learned-summary baseline, or comparison against closely related backward-model distillation/agreement objectives such as BST or MiM.

The paper does not provide a substantive limitations or ethics discussion, including licensing and privacy considerations for the large web and GitHub-derived training mixture. Overall, the idea and scale are promising, but compute fairness, reproducibility, and evaluation gaps place the work marginally below the acceptance threshold.

strengths: The paper presents a clear, intuitively motivated framework for supervising language models with summaries of longer-range future context. The manuscript is generally well organized and visually polished. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/964f8ef3a2e84c30b361c86a961dc55d/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The synthetic path-star and sibling-discovery experiments are useful for illustrating why long-horizon supervision and adaptive summaries can help in different settings.

The empirical effort is substantial: the study includes 3B- and 8B-parameter models, up to 1T training tokens, multiple seeds, several reasoning and coding benchmarks, language-modeling measurements, and data-constrained experiments.
The comparison among immediate-token, skipped-token, bag-of-words, and learned-summary targets provides informative evidence that the construction of the auxiliary target matters.
FSP-RevLM produces several meaningful improvements at 8B scale, particularly over vanilla MTP on MATH, GSM8K, and ARC-Easy, without adding inference-time components.
weaknesses: The central comparison is not compute-matched. FSP-RevLM requires training a reverse model of the same size for the same number of steps, roughly doubling total training compute, yet it is compared against NTP and MTP models receiving only the student-training budget. The claim that the teacher cost can be amortized does not replace the necessary comparison against longer-trained NTP/MTP, a larger model, or another use of the same additional compute. This is especially consequential because many reported gains are modest or inconsistent.

The empirical picture is substantially weaker at 3B scale: DS-MTP outperforms FSP-RevLM on four of six tasks, while FSP-RevLM is essentially tied with NTP on MATH and yields only small changes on several other tasks. Even at 8B, it underperforms NTP on GSM8K, its MATH advantage over NTP is small relative to the reported uncertainty, and it ties MTP on HumanEval+. Statements that it consistently improves performance or improves across math, reasoning, and coding are therefore too broad.

Novelty is limited by close predecessors. Twin Networks already matches forward hidden states to representations from a reverse sequence model, and SemFormer, Meet-in-the-Middle, belief-state models, and next-latent prediction pursue closely related future-representation supervision. Scaling this family of ideas to transformers is valuable, but the paper does not empirically compare against these closest representation-level methods, so the claimed advance over prior work remains unclear.

The mechanism is insufficiently isolated. A reverse-LM hidden state at the relevant suffix boundary is directly optimized to predict the next token, so gains may arise from reverse-model distillation rather than from a compact long-horizon summary. Missing controls include reverse-teacher logits, short or truncated suffixes, alternative bidirectional/autoencoding teachers, frozen or random features, and tests relating performance to how much genuinely distant information the target contains.

Important implementation details needed for reproducibility are absent or ambiguous, including the relative weight and normalization of the auxiliary loss, the exact auxiliary-head architecture, the precise reverse hidden state used, target normalization or stop-gradient handling, and whether targets are precomputed. Equation 7 also omits an explicit aggregation over positions. The corpus is described only at the source level, without mixture proportions, filtering, deduplication, or benchmark-contamination analysis, and no code, checkpoints, or release commitment is provided.

The evaluation protocol selects, separately for each method and task, the temperature giving the highest pass@k from eleven candidates, apparently on the reported benchmark itself. Without a separate validation set, this is test-set hyperparameter selection and can bias results. Prompting details, sample counts underlying pass@k, and uncertainty over evaluation sampling are also not adequately specified.

Figure 5 does not establish increased output diversity: higher pass@k can result from greater per-sample correctness without greater diversity. A direct diversity or solution-coverage metric, or an analysis controlling for pass@1, is required. Likewise, the data-constrained 8B result averages heterogeneous pass@1 and pass@16 scores without uncertainty and calls the setting iso-compute while excluding reverse-teacher training.

The paper frames FSP as reducing teacher forcing, but this notion is informal here and no theoretical result or direct measurement connects the auxiliary representation loss to exposure bias or autoregressive error accumulation. The large-scale evaluation also lacks long-form planning, narrative coherence, or long-context generation tasks that would directly test the motivating claims.

There is no substantive limitations, ethics, or broader-impact discussion despite very large training runs and the use of web and GitHub data, leaving computational cost, licensing, privacy, and memorization concerns unaddressed.

strengths: The idea of supervising a causal LM with compact information about a longer future is relevant, intuitive, and potentially useful.
The paper evaluates both handcrafted and learned summaries, using synthetic tasks to illustrate when long-range and adaptive summaries may help.
The 3B- and 8B-scale experiments are unusually substantial, include NTP, MTP, and DeepSeek-MTP baselines, and generally report results over three training seeds.
The appendices provide useful architecture, optimization, language-modeling, and data-constrained results.
weaknesses: The principal comparison is not compute-matched: FSP-RevLM requires training a reverse model of the same size for the same number of steps, roughly doubling total training compute. Excluding this cost as an amortized teacher overhead makes the reported improvements insufficient evidence that FSP is a more efficient or effective pretraining objective. Some data-constrained experiments are nevertheless described as iso-compute.

The empirical advantage is mixed. At 3B, DeepSeek-MTP outperforms FSP-RevLM on four of six downstream tasks; at 8B, NTP remains better on GSM8K and MTP ties FSP on HumanEval+. The claimed favorable scaling is confounded because the 3B and 8B models use different token budgets, context lengths, architectures, and training schedules.

Evaluation relies primarily on pass@16 for math and code, and the best temperature is selected separately for every method and test benchmark from eleven choices. This test-set tuning can bias results, while pass@16 emphasizes sampling diversity rather than single-sample capability. Conventional pass@1 results and evaluation with temperatures chosen on held-out development data are needed.

The paper frames FSP as reducing teacher forcing and exposure bias, but the main next-token objective remains fully teacher-forced; FSP adds an auxiliary future-distillation loss. No direct evaluation of exposure bias, compounding generation errors, long-form coherence, or the creative-writing limitations motivating the work is provided.

Novelty is limited by close predecessors. FSP-RevLM strongly resembles Twin Networks' matching of forward states to reverse-model future states, while SemFormer and prior set-level objectives already use future representations or bag-of-words supervision. Scaling the mechanism to transformers is valuable engineering evidence, but the claimed new framework does not establish a sufficiently distinct technical contribution.

Important methodological details are underspecified: Equation 7 leaves the aggregation over positions unclear and gives no coefficient balancing the auxiliary and NTP losses; the normalization and weighting of the vocabulary-sized BCE and L2 losses are absent; tf-idf construction, tokenizer and preprocessing details, exact corpus mixture weights, prompts, stopping criteria, and scoring procedures are not reported.
The training corpus includes broad GitHub and reasoning-oriented sources, but no benchmark decontamination analysis is presented. This is particularly concerning for HumanEval, MBPP, GSM8K, and MATH.

Several claims are weakly supported: the comparison to multi-head MTP at meaningful scale appears only on a synthetic task; the 'adaptive' nature of reverse summaries is supported mainly by descriptive attention plots rather than causal analysis; and the 8B data-constrained result reports only an aggregate without task-level values or uncertainty. No code, checkpoints, or exact data recipe are provided, limiting reproducibility.

strengths: The central idea—replacing position-specific future-token targets with a compact future summary—is intuitive, relevant to improving pretraining objectives, and presented clearly through both bag-of-words and learned ReverseLM variants.

The empirical effort is unusually substantial: the paper reports 3B- and 8B-parameter pretraining runs on 250B and 1T tokens, three seeds, synthetic diagnostic tasks, downstream reasoning and coding benchmarks, language-modeling evaluations, and data-constrained experiments.

At 8B scale, FSP-RevLM provides encouraging gains over NTP and one-head MTP, most notably on ARC-Easy (0.766 versus 0.718/0.736), ARC-Challenge (0.559 versus 0.531/0.552), and MBPP (0.683 versus 0.657/0.672). The path-star results also cleanly demonstrate a case where long-range summary supervision helps.

The paper is commendably transparent that FSP-RevLM requires a separately trained reverse model of equal size and therefore roughly doubles total training compute. The synthetic sibling-discovery experiment further offers a useful qualitative motivation for learned rather than indiscriminate future summaries. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/experiments/runs/20260921_han_gpt_all_anonymized_review/scratch/8910c81268414a1aa7314a71d2ec0013/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
weaknesses: The main comparison is not compute-matched. FSP-RevLM trains an additional same-size ReverseLM for the same number of steps, approximately doubling total compute, yet it is compared with NTP and MTP models trained only once. Excluding this cost by analogy with amortized distillation does not establish superior pretraining efficiency, especially because this teacher is trained specifically on the same corpus. A matched-FLOP NTP/MTP baseline is essential; the data-constrained experiment is likewise not genuinely iso-compute for FSP when teacher cost is included.

Novelty is moderate rather than decisive. The core learned variant closely resembles Twin Networks—alignment of forward states with representations from a reverse model—and is also related to SemFormer, BST, and Meet-in-the-Middle. Scaling this mechanism to modern transformers is valuable, but no direct empirical comparison isolates an advantage over these closest alternatives.

The headline empirical picture is mixed. At 3B, DS-MTP wins on four of six tasks; at 8B, FSP-RevLM loses to NTP on GSM8K, ties MTP on HumanEval+, and its MATH and MBPP advantages are small relative to reported uncertainty. Thus claims of consistent improvement and gains on long-horizon reasoning are stronger than the tables support.

Evaluation tunes decoding temperature separately for each method and benchmark and reports the best test-set pass@k, with no described validation procedure. This can inflate results through benchmark-specific selection. Moreover, pass@16 is less informative than standard pass@1 for assessing base-model quality, and the pass@k curves do not by themselves establish the claimed increase in output diversity.

The paper motivates long-form planning, narrative coherence, and creative generation, but evaluates primarily short-form ARC, math, and coding tasks. There is no direct long-context, long-form generation, plan-coherence, or error-accumulation evaluation, leaving the central long-horizon interpretation only indirectly supported.

Important implementation and ablation details are missing. Equation 7 lacks the sum over positions and an auxiliary-loss coefficient; the paper does not clearly specify stop-gradient/frozen-teacher behavior, exact ReverseLM target alignment and normalization, or target computation/storage. There are also no systematic studies of loss weight, teacher size/quality, summary horizon, or comparable multi-head MTP at large scale.

Reproducibility is limited by the incompletely specified proprietary-style training mixture: sources are named but mixture proportions, filtering/deduplication, tokenizer, sampling policy, and several optimizer/schedule details are absent. Given the enormous training budget, independent replication would be difficult.
